title: The Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Taxonomy

related.label: Markov Decision Processes and the Bellman Equation

summary: The three-way split that organizes the entire field of machine learning — supervised (learning from labeled examples), unsupervised (finding structure with no labels at all), and reinforcement (learning from reward through interaction) — and why this discipline covers the first two in depth while pointing to material already published for the third.

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Course Syllabus
Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data

title: Is Learning Feasible? Generalization and the Hoeffding Bound
summary: Before writing a single learning algorithm, the honest question this discipline opens with: can a rule learned from a finite sample of data ever be trusted to work on data it has never seen? The Hoeffding bound gives a real, quantitative answer.

references.label: Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 2: Is Learning Feasible?
Stanford CS229 — Course Syllabus

title: Training, Test, and Validation Splits
summary: The practical discipline that turns the generalization question into something you can actually measure: holding out data the model never trains on, and never touching the true test set until every other decision is already made.

references.label: James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning
Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 13: Validation

title: Linear Regression as Least Squares
summary: The single most-used model in all of statistics and machine learning, arriving here as no new mathematics at all — it is exactly the normal-equation problem already solved geometrically and via optimization in this curriculum's linear algebra discipline, now reframed as prediction on unseen data.

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Lecture Notes, Part I: Linear Regression
James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning

title: The Probabilistic View of Linear Regression
summary: Why minimizing squared error is not an arbitrary choice: assuming the noise around the true line is normally distributed, maximizing the likelihood of the observed data produces exactly the same least-squares solution already derived geometrically.

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Lecture Notes, Part I: Linear Regression
Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 3: The Linear Model I

title: Gradient Descent as a General Optimizer

related.label: Gradients: Extending Derivatives to Several Variables

summary: Turning the informal gradient already introduced in this curriculum's linear algebra discipline into a full iterative algorithm — repeatedly stepping opposite the gradient until a loss function's minimum is reached, the one optimization technique nearly every model in this discipline ultimately reduces to.

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Lecture Notes, Part I: Linear Regression
MIT 18.065 — Syllabus (OCW)

title: Logistic Regression and Decision Boundaries
summary: Adapting the linear-model-plus-gradient-descent machinery just built to a fundamentally different task — predicting a category, not a number — by squashing a linear score through a sigmoid and drawing the boundary where it crosses one-half.

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Lecture Notes, Part I: Linear Regression
James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning

title: Generative Classifiers: Gaussian Discriminant Analysis and Naive Bayes
summary: A second, genuinely different way to classify: instead of directly modeling the decision boundary (as logistic regression does), model how each class generates its data and let Bayes' theorem — already covered in full with a real diagnostic-test example — turn that into a prediction.

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Lecture Notes, Part II: Classification and Logistic Regression
James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning

title: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff
summary: Decomposing a model's prediction error into two competing sources — bias, from a model too simple to capture the true pattern, and variance, from a model so flexible it fits the noise — with a real worked numeric decomposition, not just the qualitative story.

references.label: Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 8: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning

title: Overfitting and the VC Dimension
summary: A precise measure of how much a model class can possibly overfit, before it ever sees any data — the VC dimension counts the largest set of points a model can shatter, and directly predicts how much data it takes to learn reliably.

references.label: Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 7: The VC Dimension
Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 11: Overfitting

title: Regularization: Ridge and Lasso
summary: Fighting overfitting directly by penalizing large weights in the loss function — ridge regression's smooth circular penalty shrinks every weight a little, while lasso's diamond-shaped penalty can shrink some weights to exactly zero, a real geometric difference with real consequences.

references.label: James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning
Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 12: Regularization

title: Cross-Validation
summary: Squeezing a reliable estimate of a model's true generalization error out of a single, finite dataset — k-fold cross-validation trains and validates on every possible split, then averages, so no single lucky or unlucky split decides which model wins.

references.label: James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning
Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 13: Validation

title: Evaluation Metrics: Precision, Recall, and ROC
summary: Why raw accuracy lies on imbalanced data, and the confusion-matrix-derived metrics — precision, recall, F1, and the ROC curve's true-positive-vs-false-positive tradeoff — that a real classifier must actually be judged on.

references.label: James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning
Stanford CS229 — Lecture Notes, Part II: Classification and Logistic Regression

title: Decision Trees
summary: A classifier built from nothing more exotic than the binary tree already covered as a data structure — here, each split is chosen by the feature and threshold that most reduces impurity, producing a model a human can read straight off the page.

references.label: James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning
Stanford CS229 — Course Syllabus

title: Ensembles: Bagging, Boosting, and Random Forests
summary: Combining many individually weak or overfit trees into one strong model — bagging averages many independent, high-variance trees to cancel out their noise, while boosting builds trees in sequence, each one correcting the last one's mistakes.

references.label: James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning
Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 8: Bias-Variance Tradeoff

title: Maximal-Margin Classifiers and Support Vector Machines
summary: Choosing not just any separating line between two classes, but the one with the widest possible margin on both sides — the handful of points that margin actually touches, the support vectors, are the only data the final classifier depends on.

references.label: Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 14: Support Vector Machines
James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning

title: The Kernel Trick

related.label: The Dot Product and Vector Norms

summary: Making a linear classifier separate data that is not linearly separable at all, by replacing every dot product — the one operation SVMs actually use — with a kernel function that computes the same value as if the data had been mapped into a much higher-dimensional space, without ever building that space.

references.label: Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 15: Kernel Methods
Stanford CS229 — Lecture Notes, Part I: Linear Regression

title: K-Means Clustering
summary: The first unsupervised algorithm in this discipline: with no labels at all, alternately assign each point to its nearest of k cluster centers and recompute each center as the mean of its assigned points, until nothing moves.

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Course Syllabus
James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning

title: Gaussian Mixture Models and the EM Algorithm
summary: A softer, probabilistic generalization of k-means — every point gets a probability of belonging to each of several overlapping normal distributions, fit by alternating between guessing those probabilities (E-step) and re-fitting the distributions to match (M-step).

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Course Syllabus
Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data

title: Principal Component Analysis
summary: Compressing high-dimensional data down to its most informative few directions — literally the eigenvectors of the data's own covariance matrix, the exact guarantee about symmetric matrices already proven in this curriculum's linear algebra discipline, now put to direct use.

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Course Syllabus
MIT 18.065 — Syllabus (OCW)

title: The Perceptron
summary: The oldest learning algorithm in this cluster and the direct ancestor of every neural network — a single linear threshold unit that adjusts its own weights, one misclassified example at a time, until (if the data is linearly separable) it converges exactly.

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Lecture Notes, Part I: Linear Regression
Caltech CS 156 — Learning From Data, Lecture 3: The Linear Model I

title: From Perceptrons to Neural Networks
summary: Stacking perceptron-like units into layers and replacing the hard threshold with a smooth activation function — enough to escape the single perceptron's fundamental limit of only ever drawing a straight line, and the exact point where this discipline deliberately stops, handing off to a dedicated deep learning discipline.

references.label: Stanford CS229 — Course Syllabus
James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani — An Introduction to Statistical Learning

title: Choosing and Validating a Model: A Decision Guide
summary: A capstone walkthrough comparing every model family covered in this discipline — regression, generative and discriminative classifiers, trees and ensembles, SVMs, clustering, and neural networks — by interpretability, data size, and nonlinearity, and validating the final choice end to end.
